new_statements.quote: The phonology of Ampari Pa is based on rapid observations and should therefore be regarded as tentative at this stage. [...] 3.3 Tones. Ampari Pa has two tones, High and Low, and few glides.
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger [& Denis Douyon]. 2005 [printout dated Cambridge, 8 July 2012]. Ampari Pa, a Dogon language in Northern Mali and its affinities. Draft annotated wordlist paper, Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, Cambridge. 20 pp.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3 'Phonology', p. 3 and sec. 3.3 'Tones', p. 4 (PDF pp. 4-5)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (20 pp., text layer present, the PDF's metadata: 'Ampari Pa wordlist paper', created 8 July 2012). Both quoted sentences are verbatim at the stated locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 3) 'The phonology of Ampari Pa is based on rapid observations and should therefore be regarded as tentative at this stage.' and PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4) '3.3 Tones / Ampari Pa has two tones, High and Low, and few glides.' I read the whole of sec. 3 (3.1 seven vowels with length and nasalisation, 3.2 consonant chart with free voicing variation and a trilled rr, 3.3 the one-line tone statement) and sec. 4-5; a full-text search for stress/accent finds no token 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' or 'pitch' anywhere…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only Ampari-specific phonological description states a two-tone (H, L) system with few contour tones; it says nothing about word stress or accent. Heath's comparative note (2015: 3) adds that in Ampari, as in the other southwestern Dogon languages, verb tones are fully determined by inflectional category (no lexical verb melodies). No source describes stress placement in Ampari.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement based on a one-day ('one-shot') wordlist elicitation in Pa (Pahandaga) village, 7 March 2005; isolation/citation forms; the author flags the phonology as tentative.
new_statements.identity_note: The only Ampari-specific phonology (Blench & Douyon 2005) describes the lect of Pa (= Pahandaga) village, an isolated eastern outlier of Ampari surrounded by Tomo Kan speakers, which Blench calls 'a dialect of Ampari' at 'the extreme end of the continuum that includes the Ampari and Mombo groups'; Glottolog ampa1238 has no dialect subdivisions, so it falls under ampa1238. The Dogon and Bangime Linguistics project's Ampari data (Prokhorov) come from the Nando/Baboye area. Other names: Ampari-kora (Hochstetler et al. 2004), ãmbãŋge / Ambeenge (Calame-Griaule 1956), grouped with Mombo under the exonym Kolum So / 'Pignari'. Penange (pena1270), Mombo (momb1254) and Bunoge (buno1241) grammars were opened for context only and are not Ampari.

sources.note: Mombo is Ampari's closest documented relative (Blench: Pa 'certainly closer to Mombo than any neighbouring Dogon lects'); a complete phonology chapter would give the nearest proxy statement on stress/accent for the Mombo-Ampari group, though it would not be an Ampari statement.

sources.note: About Penange only (no stress/accent system distinguishing clitics; variable phonetic initial-syllable stress in isolation forms). On Ampari it says only that Prokhorov 'specializes in Mombo and Ampari' (sec. 1.4.1); no Ampari description cited.

sources.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015 (last update December 2014). Dogon lexical tones of stems. Unpublished typology document, Dogon and Bangime Linguistics project. 6 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement for Ampari. p. 3: 'In southwestern Dogon (Bunoge, Penange, Ampari, Mombo) and in Tiranige (northwestern), all verb forms have tones that are predictable from the inflectional form, so there are no lexical melodies.' (Donno So is separately described as 'semi-accentual'/'pitch accent', not Ampari.)
